html:
A University of Nottingham professor with a big following online, Mike Pound of the Computerphile YouTube channel, explains DeepSeek and how it compares with ChatGPT. In some ways the comparison looks a lot like GPU versus CPU. (If you’d rather not watch the video, scroll straight down to the summary at the end )

Here is roughly what he says:

Another day, another AI model. So why does this one matter so much? We don’t make many videos about new AI model releases, because there are so many of them and a lot of them aren’t that interesting. But in the last few days a model called DeepSeek has come out, along with a new one called DeepSeek R1, and they are really interesting. I think they genuinely threaten some companies’ monopoly on this kind of system.

For anyone meeting this for the first time, let’s start with what a large language model is. A large language model is a very large, Transformer-based neural network that does next-word prediction. Since around 2017, Transformers have been a major milestone in generative AI.

To make sense of the jargon, we need a few basic concepts. Neural networks are a standard approach in machine learning; convolutional networks, for example, are very popular in image-based computer vision. The way you train these models is that you start with a huge model, far too big for most of us. You might need hundreds of thousands of GPUs (graphics cards) to train it. Then you feed it batch after batch of all the text on the internet, learning over and over again how to predict the next word, until you get really good at it.

What has happened over the past few years is an arms race among all the tech companies to see who can build the biggest model and who can build the best-performing one. Broadly, their approach has been to make the models bigger, make the datasets bigger, make them smarter, and keep training until performance improves.

If you have 100,000 graphics cards and billions of dollars to spend, you have the advantage. Some companies, like OpenAI, keep their models behind the curtain. They expose them through an API or a web interface and rarely release them to anyone. They also rarely tell you how they trained the model, what the dataset was, what the actual model parameters are, or how big it is.

On the other hand, companies like Meta (the company behind Facebook) have a much more open AI policy. They basically release their models, called Llama, which are very good, free, and available to everyone. But whether or not the models are released, they are beyond the reach of most people. I can run these models and I can improve them, but I can’t train them, because I don’t have those kinds of resources. I don’t have the money to pay the electricity bill for a server farm.

In most fields of science, you might read a paper and think, that’s good, but I think I can change it and make it better, and then you publish a paper showing you’ve done better than they did. That doesn’t happen much with large AI models, because in the end only a handful of people can do it.

Just before the end of last year, a Chinese company released the DeepSeek models, and they really have changed the game, because they essentially show that you can train with much more limited hardware. It’s still expensive, but far less constrained. The latest variant in particular is much more efficient in how much data it needs to collect.

Let’s talk about V3 first, their flagship model. You can think of it as something a bit like ChatGPT. It’s basically another big Transformer trained on a lot of text. It can hold a conversation: you can talk to it, and it gives very sensible answers. You can use it online now.

The people who trained it claim the model performs similarly to Llama and ChatGPT, but needed only $5 million worth of hardware and electricity. For comparison, one of the biggest models might have cost more than a hundred million, maybe even a billion dollars. And you have to remember that you probably won’t get it right the first time; you may be training several variants.

But the more interesting one is the R1 model, which does something called chain of thought. The observation behind chain of thought is this: if you ask it a math problem, or a language problem, or for the definition of something in physics, it doesn’t just answer. It also shows the reasoning it went through to solve the problem.

Traditionally, training a model like this takes a huge amount of training data with detailed, worked-out solution steps, and that is hard to come by. R1 takes an innovative approach: it is trained with reinforcement learning. You only need to give it the questions and the answers, and a reward mechanism encourages it to produce a sensible reasoning process. That makes training far easier, because nobody has to write out the detailed reasoning steps by hand.

Most importantly, they have released all of it as open-source software. Suddenly, that means you can do this at home. You still need a lot of graphics cards, but very few compared with before. An organization the size of a university can now do this quite comfortably.

The implications for the industry are profound. Companies with huge numbers of GPUs may keep their advantage for a while, but over time things will even out, and people will be able to do a lot with more limited hardware. That will make for a more level playing field, and we may see more innovative companies emerge and find new efficiency gains.

In the end we may see the end of closed-source AI, because if open-source models can reach similar performance at lower cost, there is not much point in keeping models closed. This shift could democratize AI technology further and let many more players take part in its development.

Key points

1. Why the DeepSeek models matter

  • DeepSeek V3 and R1 challenge the current monopoly in AI
  • Much lower training cost: the flagship model cost only $5 million to train (conventional models cost hundreds of millions to a billion dollars)
  • An open-source strategy that democratizes the technology, so universities and mid-sized organizations can also take part in AI development

2. Key technical breakthroughs

  • V3: performance on a par with ChatGPT and Llama, with far lower hardware requirements
  • R1:
    • Chain of thought (it shows how it solves a problem)
    • A novel reinforcement-learning approach to training: it needs only question–answer pairs, with no hand-annotated reasoning steps
    • Breaks the traditional dependence on massive annotated datasets

3. Impact on the industry

  • Breaks the closed-source monopoly: open-source models come close to closed systems in performance, undermining the very basis of the commercial closed-source model
  • Lower resource barriers: from “a hundred thousand GPUs plus a billion dollars” to “thousands of GPUs plus a few million dollars”
  • A catalyst for an innovation ecosystem: more small and mid-sized teams can iterate on models, speeding up the democratization of the technology

4. Predicted trends

  • Closed-source AI may gradually retreat from general-purpose applications, with open-source models dominating the market
  • Competition shifts from “scale of compute” to “algorithmic efficiency”
  • New business models emerge (fine-tuning services, domain-specific AI and so on)

Bottom line: With its one-two-three punch of low-cost training, chain-of-thought innovation and full open-sourcing, DeepSeek is rewriting the rules of the AI industry, and could set off an upheaval like the one Linux brought to operating systems.
